item.title: Baby survives fall from third-storey window in Amsterdam
item.description:
Baby survives fall from third-storey window in Amsterdam

November 23, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A baby who fell from a third-storey window in Amsterdam survived the incident, police have revealed.

The one-year-old boy was found lying on the ground on the evening of October 30 by a passer-by on Amstelveenweg.

Police are still investigating how the child fell and have appealed for witnesses or anybody in the area with video footage to contact them.

The boy was taken to hospital after the incident. Police did not disclose any details of his condition.

item.title: NL sends delegation to India over abducted Amsterdam girl
item.description:
NL sends delegation to India over abducted Amsterdam girl

November 23, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch government is sending a delegation of officials to India this week to push for the return of Insiya, a girl from Amsterdam who was abducted on her father’s orders 10 years ago.

Foreign minister Tom Berendsen, who happens to be on a working visit to India, told broadcaster NOS that officials from the foreign and justice ministries will discuss what legal options are available, including the Netherlands’ request to extradite her father, Shehzad Hemani.

He said he hopes the delegation can take the first steps towards restoring contact between Insiya and her mother, Nadia Rashid, who has not seen her daughter since 2016.

Insiya was two years old when she was taken from her grandmother’s home in Amsterdam-Oost in 2016 by a group of men hired by her father. They took her to India via Germany using false documents. She is now 12.

A Dutch court sentenced Hemani in absentia to 8.5 years in prison. Several of his accomplices were jailed for up to four years. India has not extradited Hemani and has not signed the international treaty on child abduction. Indian courts do not treat a child’s removal as abduction if the child lives with one of the parents.

The delegation’s trip follows a video message to Insiya that Amsterdam mayor Femke Halsema posted on social media on Sunday. The video is an attempt to get round an Indian court order that has hidden hundreds of articles about the case from users in India.

Since October 30, Google has blocked publications about Insiya for users in India, following an order by a court in New Delhi, NOS reported. The case was brought in the girl’s name by her father and grandmother, who cited safety concerns.

The block covers Dutch and international media reports, Dutch court press releases, government documents and Rashid’s social media accounts, which she had used to try to reach her daughter.

Halsema put out a video message while on a trade mission in Mumbai last week, in which Insiya’s mother tells her daughter that she misses her. Halsema encouraged people to share the video widely.

item.title: PvdD marks 20 years in parliament fighting factory farming
item.description:
PvdD marks 20 years in parliament fighting factory farming

November 23, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Animal rights party PvdD celebrated its 20th year in parliament yesterday, two decades after it became the first political party on earth to gain such power under the banner of improving livestock welfare and banning factory farming.

Party leader Christine Teunissen addressed a crowd of members in Nieuwegein, Utrecht, saying that the group has grown to be “the thorn in the side of the ruling powers”, according to broadcaster NOS.

She drew attention to the leverage the PvdD achieved during the recent cabinet crisis, in which the Jetten government managed to pass its tax plan with essential support from the party, who lent its backing in return for (among other things) funding for alternatives to animal testing.

Teunissen said it she was proud that the PvdD could “break through the VVD’s power politics”, and had shown “what is possible when the VVD is not in control”.

The right-wing liberal VVD voted against its coalition partners, centrist D66 and Christian Democrat CDA, after they agreed a new tax proposal with left-wing opposition parties. This sparked a crisis that many feared would collapse the government.

The PvdD originally refused to support the plan, but its 3 seats in parliament became pivotal amid the dispute.

A bill on livestock farming, which addresses the party’s founding purpose, is due to be voted on in December. It would effectively ban factory farming by 2040, ensuring that all animals are kept in conditions that respect their natural behaviours.

There is already a government act in place that seeks to ensure the same ends, but the PvdD maintains it is too weak to be realistic. A separate bill on banning cruel slaughter methods is also in the works.

item.title: Prosecutors ask for 30 years and treatment for Erasmus shooter
item.description:
Prosecutors ask for 30 years and treatment for Erasmus shooter

November 23, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Prosecutors have demanded a 30-year sentence on appeal for a medical student who shot dead two of his neighbours and a teacher in a fit of “uncontrollable rage”.

Faoud L., from Rotterdam, was given a life sentence for the triple murder at his original trial in February last year.

The public prosecution service said a fixed term was more appropriate because it would allow L. to be given a compulsory treatment order. L. is also appealing against the sentence.

The trial judge said therapy was unlikely to be effective after 30 years in prison, whereas a prisoner on a life sentence can apply for parole after 25 years.

L. shot his next-door neighbour, a 39-year-old woman named as Marlous, and her 14-year-old daughter, Romy, in September 2023, before setting his own flat on fire.

He then rode his motorcycle to Rotterdam’s Erasmus Medical Centre where he shot dead 43-year-old Jurgen Damen as he was giving a lecture to a class of students.

L., now 35, was studying medicine at the university, but became enraged when the exams committee refused to let him sit for his diploma unless he underwent a psychological assessment.

He told an earlier court hearing that he originally planned to kill several students in the classroom, but persuaded himself to target only the lecturer after an “internal conflict”.

Researchers at the Pieter Baan Centrum, which carries out psychological assessments on criminal suspects, concluded that he had a type of autism that made it difficult to process and recognise emotions.

item.title: How much Dutch do you need to get hired in 2027?
item.description:
Partner content

How much Dutch do you need to get hired in 2027?

November 23, 2026

“Native Dutch” in every vacancy? Here’s how to get hired anyway:

New year, new job hunt! But two little words keep stopping internationals in their tracks. Here’s why they don’t have to stop you.

“Is it even worth trying?” Jamila Vriesman, founder of Amstel Dutch, hears it all the time. Her Dutch language & culture school in Amsterdam has one simple belief: you can’t really learn Dutch without understanding the Dutch. So her students learn both.

Lately, many of them share the same story. Months of lessons. A shiny new CV. Then they spot “native Dutch” in a vacancy and close the tab faster than you can say gezellig.

“I get it,” says Jamila, a born Amsterdammer. “But please don’t give up. The market has changed. So your strategy needs to change too.”

Harder, not hopeless
Short answer: it’s not just you. Since autumn 2025, job seekers in the Netherlands have outnumbered vacancies. The latest CBS figures show 92 vacancies for every 100 job seekers.

“When employers can choose, language often tips the balance,” Jamila explains. Every month you wait, the pile of CVs next to yours grows. And more of them say “some Dutch”. The good news? This is a tiebreaker you can train for.

“Native” is a signal, not a stop sign
“Native Dutch” tells you how important the language is in the job. “Honestly, ‘native’ is an unfortunate requirement,” says Jamila. “Most employers mean professional fluency: you can follow a fast meeting and write a clear email. That is something you can learn. Being born here is not.” Tick the other boxes? Apply. Be honest about your level and show how you are working on it.

And “Dutch is a plus”? “That is not a wall,” Jamila points out. “That is an open door. Walk through it!”

Show what you’ve got
For many other jobs, you don’t need to be fluent to stand out. “Imagine 200 people apply and 15 of them speak some Dutch,” Jamila suggests. “Who do you think gets noticed? Even A2 tells an employer: I’m planning to stay.”

And A2 is closer than you think. With a busy job and one lesson a week, many people get there in about 12 months. More time? You’ll go even faster.

So show it off. Write your LinkedIn summary in Dutch. Add a short Dutch paragraph to your cover letter. Start your interview with a warm goedemorgen (good morning). “Nobody expects you to discuss tax law in your first sentence,” Jamila laughs. “But that one word already does a lot of work.”

Know your world
Every sector sets its own bar. According to Indeed, Dutch is a must in healthcare, education and law, while many tech teams mostly work in English. Know which world you’re walking into, and learn the Dutch it speaks.

Survive your first Dutch meeting
An interview follows a script. A team meeting does not. Suddenly you are in a room full of jokes, shortcuts and half sentences, nodding along and hoping nobody asks you anything. Sound familiar?

“And when a Dutch colleague calls your plan interessant, it’s not always a compliment,” Jamila smiles.

Her tip: train your ears, not just your mouth. Pick two lifesaver phrases and use them this week: Kun je dat nog een keer zeggen? (Could you say that again?) and Wat bedoel je precies? (What exactly do you mean?). Small sentences, big difference.

Find your crew
Can you do all this on your own? Partly. Apps are great for words. But they won’t tell you why your colleague went quiet after your feedback. “A teacher hears the mistakes you no longer notice,” Jamila believes. “And a group gives you a safe place to get things wrong before you do it in a meeting.”

Her last tip: stop comparing yourself to native speakers. “Compare yourself to who you were a year ago. Every level opens more doors. Companies don’t just want someone who can do the job. They want someone who’ll stay and feel at home. Language is the door. Culture is the room behind it.”

Ready to stop nodding along? Jamila and her team at Amstel Dutch teach you the language and the unwritten rules of Dutch working life. No boring drills. No stuffy classrooms.

During the Dutch City Experiences, you explore Amsterdam with your group, use your Dutch where it actually happens and end with a drink in a bruin café. Think of it as a dress rehearsal for your first coffee break at a new job. And to keep the conversation going, join the free monthly taalcafé and practise your Dutch in a relaxed setting.

In a hurry or ready to immerse yourself? Amstel Dutch also offers intensive weeks that take you through a full level in one week (coffee included, sleep optional): A0 to A1 from 14 to 19 December and A1 to A2 from 11 to 16 January 2027. More dates follow throughout the year.

Not sure where to start? Book your free 20-minute intake: you’ll know your level, the level your next job asks for, and the quickest realistic route between the two. Your way into Dutch life starts here.

item.title: Dutch households turning down gas as global unrest stokes prices
item.description:
Dutch households turning down gas as global unrest stokes prices

November 23, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Dutch households are using less gas for heating and more electricity in response to the steep rise in energy prices, according to figures from energy supplier Essent.

The company said gas consumption dropped by 10% year-on-year at the start of November, despite the cold start to the month, while electricity use was up by 40%.

Essenty said there was a clear trend towards switching to electric heating systems such as infrared panels and air conditioning units, which can also be used for heating.

Households are still using gas as their main source of heating, but electric heaters are being used as a top-up supply, with a surge in demand in the early hours of the evening as people come home from work and school.

Most homes are still connected to the gas mains, but the Dutch government is committed to switching off the supply completely by 2050.

“Under normal temperatures we saw the same gas use as normal, but op November 3, when it was 1 degree below the normal temperature, we saw 4% less gas use,” Essent energy market specialist Denise van Zon told NOS.

Earlier surveys by Essent found that a quarter of households are planning to use electric heating devices as gas prices are expected to remain high through the winter because of the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, which is restricting global supplies.

“I think the unrest is the reason for the increase,” Van Zon said. “We’ve heard about the gas reserves, the conflict in Iran and we have seen another significant increase in prices.”

The average household gas price has risen by 35% since October last year and many energy companies are offering lower prices for multiple-year contracts in an attempt to encourage customers to fix their prices for the long term.

item.title: Dutch man who spent 42 years in US prison for murder dies
item.description:
Dutch man who spent 42 years in US prison for murder dies

November 23, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A Dutch man who spent 42 years in prison in the US for murder has died of leukaemia, eight months after being repatriated to the Netherlands.

Jaitsen Singh, 81, spent his final months in Scheveningen after the appeal court in The Hague ordered the government to bring him home because of his age and ill health.

His death on Sunday was confirmed in an online post by his lawyer, Rachel Imamkhan, who represented him since 2011. He was the longest serving Dutch prisoner in foreign custody.

“Those who knew him will mainly remember the man behind the case,” she wrote.

In August the appeal court ordered him to be transferred from the US to the Netherlands, following years of campaigning by his family and lawyers.

He was born in Suriname when it was still a Dutch colony and held a Dutch passport, even after moving to the US in 1970. The Dutch attorney general opposed his repatriation, arguing he had insufficient ties to the country.

Denied guilt

Singh was jailed in 1986 for “56 years to life” for arranging the murder of his wife and stepdaughter, but he has always denied committing the crime.

Their bodies were found in the boot of their car in Los Angeles two years earlier. A key piece of evidence was a statement by a serving prisoner who was later found to have been bribed.

Imamkhan said his case was “seen by many as a miscarriage of justice in the United States and remained a subject of debate for years.”

But the family of his wife and stepdaughter said they believed he was responsible for their deaths and his “‘continued denial and lack of remorse have only deepened the family’s suffering”.

In a statement released through the family support organisation Namens de Familie, they said Singh was being portrayed as a victim “while two innocent lives that have been taken away are once again fading into the background.”

Last August the appeal court ordered the state to request Singh’s transfer from the US to a Dutch prison, following years of campaigning by his family and lawyers. He flew into the Netherlands in March this year.

He was born in Suriname when it was still a Dutch colony and held a Dutch passport, even after moving to the US in 1970. The Netherlands opposed his repatriation, arguing he had insufficient ties to the country.

item.title: US turtle invasion: exotic species spreading through NL
item.description:
US turtle invasion: exotic species spreading through NL

November 23, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

An “invasive exotic species” in spreading through the Netherlands – the yellow-bellied slider turtle – which has been brought from the US and can now survive in an increasingly warm environment, according to radio programme Vroege Vogels.

The species has long been imported from America and sold as pets but until recently could not survive in the cold Dutch climate.

This has changed and last Spring someone spotted a group of young turtles by a pond in Zuid-Holland, and contacted Faunawatch, an organisation dedicated to abandoned turtles.

After inspecting the site, sixteen empty eggs and two young turtles were found, both of which have been taken to a rescue centre in Limburg.

Tim Huijsmans, a researcher from Faunawatch, told the radio programme that climate change is making it possible for these turtles to breed in the Netherlands for the first time.

“If it is too cold, the hatchlings die in the egg. So now, for the first time, young water turtles have been born. After hatching, they burrowed into the ground during the winter and went to the water in the spring,” he explained.

An estimated 200,000 freshwater turtles have been dumped in the Dutch wild, he said, and the government now needs to allocate funds to monitor their spread and the risks associated.

item.title: Jetten and Burnham pledge to keep up support for Ukraine
item.description:
Jetten and Burnham pledge to keep up support for Ukraine

November 23, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Prime minister Rob Jetten and his British counterpart Andy Burnham have pledged to keep up support for Ukraine as Burnham made his first official visit to the Netherlands since taking office in July.

The two leaders also discussed last week’s summit between the UK and the European Union in Brussels as Burnham tries to rebuild relations with continental Europe after Brexit.

In a post on social media site X, Jetten said he valued the “long and close” relationship between the two countries as “neighbours, allies and partners in Europe”.

“Our countries have worked together for years for a stronger and safer Europe,” Jetten said. “It is a pleasure to build on that co-operation together with Andy Burnham”.

Burnham said he and Jetten “agreed on the vital need to keep the pressure up on Russia to bring Putin to the negotiations table” and the two countries would continue to support Ukraine in order to “secure a lasting, durable peace”.

In a statement on the UK government website, he also thanked the Dutch prime minister for his support in securing what he called “a win-win deal for Britain and the EU.”

As part of the deal agreed in Brussels, the two sides agreed to scrap most border checks on agricultural exports and allow up to 100,000 young people to move across the border to live and work for up to three years.

The Netherlands is the UK’s third largest trading partner, account for 6.3% of British trade. Dutch foreign direct investment in the UK makes up 9.4% of the total.

Jetten and Burnham had dinner in the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam on Saturday evening, together with Jetten’s fiancé Nicolas Keenan and Burnham’s Dutch wife, Marie-France van Heel.

On Sunday the British prime minister was in Rotterdam, where he watched AZ beat Sparta 5-1, accompanied by mayor Carola Schouten.

item.title: Offline, on the floor and in the sauna
item.description:
Offline, on the floor and in the sauna

November 23, 2026 Molly Quell

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

While much of Amsterdam was enjoying a night out at a bar or restaurant on a Saturday evening, on a boat on the IJ, a group was listening to the dulcet tones of a clarinet while wrapped in bathrobes.

Stoom Goes Deeper is the brainchild of entrepreneur Sjoerd Schaap, whose latest venture is a sauna and hotel aboard a former paddle steamer docked at the NDSM wharf.

It’s “an evening of sound, breath and heat,” Schaap told Dutch News.

I received an invitation to attend the event after Schaap read my column about surviving a Dutch sauna experience, which I guess makes me Dutch News’ official Sauna Correspondent.

You can find Kapitein Anna at the end of the pier, just past the Botel. The ship, built in 1911, now has 14 hotel rooms and multiple saunas. If you’ve ever taken the ferry to Amsterdam Noord and wondered why there are a lot of people lounging around in swimwear, you’re looking into Stoom’s main sauna.

The stern of the boat has been turned entirely into a sauna with a view of Amsterdam Centraal and the Pontsteiger.

Bucking Dutch tradition, swimwear is required. “We want everyone to feel included,” Schaap said.

Stoom Goes Deeper was in its second edition when I attended.

Around 40 people from a variety of ages and nationalities spread out on yoga mats or on the lounge seating on Kapitein Anna’s main deck. Most wore bathrobes and sweatpants. They tucked themselves into towels and blankets.

The evening was emceed by Joep Mencke, a DJ and “breathwork facilitator.” For about 90 minutes, Mencke played relaxing tunes, accompanied by a clarinetist, and instructed the group through a series of breathing exercises.

Afterwards, everyone went into the sauna.

It’s “a moment to step away from the everyday and reconnect with yourself,” said Schaap.

I am not a person who is especially into meditation, and my engineer husband was skeptical of the “journey”, as Mencke described it, but lying around, with no phone, listening to lovely music was a delightful way to spend a Saturday evening.

“Breathwork has really helped me, it helps me relax, it takes me to another place where I can process things,” Claire Hoekstra told Dutch News. She had come to the event with a friend.

Most of the attendees came in pairs – there were a lot of couples – or small groups. But several came by themselves. Schaap bills the event as a “social sauna” and several people introduce themselves to one another. Two men were even exchanging business cards as they were leaving.

There is a bar as well, including lots of hydrating and electrolyte-filled options for anyone sweating it out.

The highlight for me was the sauna. The view onto the IJ at night is gorgeous and there’s a real thrill of sitting in a sauna, watching the ferries dock and depart.

Schaap intends to continue the events after the success of the first two. But if Stoom Goes Deeper doesn’t sound up your alley, the sauna facilities are open during the day as well.

I stayed in the hotel for the evening rather than ruining my relaxation on a night train. Standing outside in the fresh air on the ferry ride back to the station, I watched the Kapitein Anna as we passed. The sauna wasn’t yet open.

Maybe the next event should be Stoom Goes Earlier.
